title: Three dying declarations that don't match

scenes.dialogue: Before she died, a woman gave three statements. One named only her mother-in-law. The other two named all four in the family. Which one would you believe?
The Sessions Court acquitted her husband and his family. The High Court believed just the first statement, and gave the mother-in-law life imprisonment. So who was right?
Hi, I'm Ravishankar from LawWorld. On fifth November, twenty twenty six, Honourable Justice Ujjal Bhuyan and Honourable Justice Atul S Chandurkar ruled.
scenes.shown: Hi, I'm Ravishankar from LawWorld. On 5 November 2026, Honourable Justice Ujjal Bhuyan and Honourable Justice Atul S. Chandurkar ruled.

scenes.dialogue: The prosecution said her husband and his family ill-treated her over dowry, and because she had no child. She suffered burns at home and died five days later.
A doctor at the hospital recorded the first. A police officer and a Special Executive Magistrate took the other two, which named all four accused.
The Sessions Court found the statements did not match. The man who put out the fire and took her to hospital was never called as a witness, nor was any neighbour.
The High Court found the doctor's record voluntary. By the family's own defence, it said, the mother-in-law alone was at home with her, and gave no explanation.

scenes.dialogue: Finally, what did the Supreme Court decide? Given the inconsistency in the three statements, the Sessions Court was right. She was entitled to the benefit of doubt.
Her acquittal had strengthened the presumption of innocence, and the doctor's record, without corroboration, could not alone reverse it. So she was acquitted.
